name: Lambrusco

lines.s10: Lambrusco is the frothy red of Modena: violet, sour cherry and wild strawberry, sharp and cool, made to cut through rich pork.
lines.s20: Lambrusco is a family of grapes from Emilia, around Modena, made into a red wine with bubbles. Pale Sorbara is sharp, with violet and sour cherry, and dark Grasparossa brings blackberry and a firmer grip.
lines.s45: Lambrusco foams in the glass, a red wine with bubbles from the plain and foothills around Modena and Reggio Emilia. It is a family of grapes, not one. Sorbara is pale and sharp, with violet and sour cherry, while Grasparossa is dark, with blackberry and a firmer grip. The acidity is high and the tannin light. The bubbles are usually made in a sealed tank, and it comes dry, off dry or sweet. Pour it cool with prosciutto, mortadella and Parmigiano, the food of its own country. Its name is thought to come from labrusca, the Romans' word for a wild vine at the edge of a field.
lines.sale: Lambrusco is a red that refreshes like a sparkling wine, all sour cherry and foam, and it was made for cured pork. Bring a cool bottle of dry Sorbara with the charcuterie board.

glass.lead: Sour cherry, wild strawberry and violet in a frothy red, pale and sharp from Sorbara, dark with blackberry and a firmer grip from Grasparossa.

ladder.where: The clay foothills of Castelvetro, as Grasparossa
The sandy plain of Sorbara, and Carpi for Salamino

glass.structure: Dry to sweet, usually gently sparkling. Acidity high, tannin low to medium, alcohol low to medium, body light to medium; pale pink to deep purple.

home.home: Emilia, around Modena and Reggio: the sandy plain of Sorbara, the clay foothills of Castelvetro and the plain round Carpi each give their own Lambrusco and their own DOC. Across the Po, Lambrusco Mantovano is Lombardy's. Most is made sparkling in a sealed tank.
home.abroad: Lambrusco Maestri, one member of the family, has travelled as far as Argentina and Australia; elsewhere it is barely grown.

service.temp: 50 to 57 degrees Fahrenheit, 10 to 14 degrees Celsius: pale Sorbara cooler, dark Grasparossa warmer.
service.glass: A white wine glass or a tulip, so the perfume and the violet foam show.
service.decant: No. Open it cool and pour it at once; the sparkle fades fast once opened.
service.age: Drink it young, within a year or two of the harvest.

with.why: bubbles and acidity cut the fat and salt
Grasparossa's firmer grip for rich, fatty pork
acidity and foam against salt and crystal
a cool, frothy red against smoke and chilli

labels.means: Dry, off dry to medium sweet, and sweet: the words that tell you the sugar.
The pale, sharp member of the family, at least 60 per cent Sorbara; its own DOC since 1970.
The dark, firmer Lambrusco of the foothills south of Modena, at least 85 per cent Grasparossa.
Frizzante is gently sparkling, the usual Lambrusco; spumante is fully sparkling.
Refermented in the bottle and left on its yeast: cloudy, dry and a little bready.

guest.a: It can be, but at home in Modena it is mostly drunk dry. Look for secco on the label; amabile is off dry to medium sweet and dolce is sweet.

guest.q: A red with bubbles? Should it be cold?
guest.a: Cool rather than icy: a pale Sorbara about as cold as a white, a dark Grasparossa a touch warmer. The chill and the foam keep it fresh beside rich food.
A family of several. Sorbara is pale and sharp, Grasparossa dark and firmer, Salamino deep and round, and each has its own DOC around Modena.

compare.tell: Barbera shares the high acidity and low tannin but is still, with black cherry and a balsamic note; Lambrusco foams, with violet and wild strawberry.
Gamay is still, with kirsch and sometimes banana from whole bunch fermentation; Lambrusco foams and bites harder, with wild strawberry and a sharp, frothy finish.
Glera, as Prosecco, is white, with green apple, pear and acacia blossom; Lambrusco is red, with sour cherry and violet, though both get their bubbles in a tank.

profile.st: Pale pink to deep purple, frothy · Body light to medium · Acid high · Tannin low to medium · Alcohol low to moderate · Dry to sweet
profile.fruit: Sour cherry, wild strawberry and raspberry in Sorbara; blackberry and black plum in Grasparossa
profile.other: Violet and rose petal; bread dough and yeast where refermented in bottle; a frothy, foaming sparkle
profile.tell: A sparkling red with a violet foam, sharp acidity and little tannin: sour cherry and violet when pale, blackberry when dark
profile.regions: Emilia around Modena and Reggio: Sorbara, Castelvetro, and Santa Croce near Carpi; Mantua in Lombardy
profile.confuse: Sparkling Shiraz is fuller, riper and darker; Brachetto d'Acqui is sweet and rose scented; Barbera shares the acidity but not the foam

cards.front: Lambrusco: name the three DOCs of 1970 around Modena and each style.
cards.back: Sorbara, pale and sharp; Grasparossa di Castelvetro, dark and firmer; Salamino di Santa Croce, deep and round. The broader Modena and Reggiano DOCs blend the family.

cards.front: On a Lambrusco label, what do secco, amabile and dolce mean?
cards.back: Dry; off dry to medium sweet; sweet. At home in Modena, dry Lambrusco is the tradition.

cards.front: Lambrusco: how are the bubbles in most bottles made?
cards.back: By a second fermentation in a sealed tank, the Charmat or Martinotti method, stopped by chilling when the fizz and the sweetness are right. Some is refermented in the bottle.

questions.q: A frothy red poured cool is pale ruby, almost pink, with violet, sour cherry and wild strawberry, sharp acidity and almost no tannin. Which Lambrusco is it?
questions.exp: Pale colour, violet and sharp acidity mark Sorbara, the pale member of the family. Salamino, the nearest miss, is deeper in colour and rounder, and Grasparossa darker and firmer still.

questions.q: A guest orders Lambrusco with the charcuterie but says she dislikes sweet wine. Which word do you look for on the label?
questions.exp: Secco means dry. Amabile, the nearest miss, is off dry to medium sweet, and dolce is sweet; frizzante speaks of the sparkle, not the sugar.

questions.q: A table orders zampone, a rich pork sausage served with lentils, and asks for a Lambrusco with enough grip for it. Which do you bring?
questions.exp: Grasparossa is the dark, firmer Lambrusco of the foothills, the local match for zampone and cotechino. Salamino, the nearest miss, is deep in colour but round and soft; Sorbara is pale and sharp.

report: Mode home and kind family, as the plan fixes them; a new grape, so the entry gives the profile and the targets (emilia-romagna, lombardy and italy, the three REGIONS.join.grapes already names).

The three DOCs of 1970 (Sorbara at least 60 per cent Sorbara with Salamino making up the rest, Grasparossa di Castelvetro at least 85 per cent, Salamino di Santa Croce around Carpi), the Reggiano and Modena DOCs, Lambrusco Mantovano in Lombardy, the tank method with bottle refermentation returning, secco, amabile and dolce, Sorbara pale and sharp with violet, Grasparossa dark and tannic for zampone and cotechino, Salamino deep and round, and serving it cold with salumi and Parmigiano all stand on the Codex's Emilia-Romagna and Lombardy records.

The serving temperature (about 10 degrees Celsius for Sorbara and the rosés, about 14 for the dark wines) stands on Gambero Rosso's guidelines for restaurateurs as search results quoted them; the Codex's own line says cold, and the amabile well chilled.

The name from labrusca, the Romans' wild vine at the edge of a field, stands on the Enoteca Regionale, Falstaff and a University of Modena and Reggio Emilia glossary; the line says is thought to come from, as the sources call it uncertain. Lambrusco Maestri in Argentina and Australia stands on Falstaff and a German wine glossary.

The ladder follows the family's members by site, as the Codex's Emilia record splits them: the foothills, which that record calls a little cooler and better aired than the plain, grow the dark Grasparossa, and the plain the pale Sorbara and the round Salamino. The change in the glass is the grape more than the climate.

Rose petal beside violet rests on trade descriptions of Sorbara; the Codex names violet alone. One Creole dish is offered, gumbo with andouille, on the strength of the Codex's own pairing of a dry Sorbara with a chilli dish; a checker may cut it.

checked.verdict: Sound after six fixes. A family and not one grape, the three DOCs of 1970, Sorbara at least 60 per cent and Grasparossa at least 85, Mantovano in Lombardy, the tank method with bottle refermentation returning and secco, amabile and dolce all stand on the Codex's Emilia and Lombardy records; violet sat on the wrong member, the grip question had a second arguable key and a card said three DOCs around Modena where the record adds the broader Modena DOC.
changed: glass.ladder: The Codex's Emilia record scents Sorbara, the pale wine of the sandy plain, with violets, and the ladder gave violet to the dark Grasparossa of the foothills. Violet moves to the plain's rung. The rungs keep the member at each site in their where, since the change in the glass is the grape's more than the climate's, as the author said.

worlds.home.abroad: The name is barely seen elsewhere is untrue of the wine, which is sold far from Emilia; it is the grape that is barely grown. Lambrusco Maestri in Argentina and Australia stands on Falstaff and the Wein.plus glossary.
compare.0.tell: Deeper did not hold against Grasparossa, which this entry itself calls dark; Barbera's balsamic note, in the Barbera entry and not in this one, now parts them with the foam.

cards.0: Its three DOCs around Modena left out the broader Modena DOC, which the Codex's Emilia record names beside Reggiano. The front now asks for the three of 1970, and the back names the broader two in place of the date the front now gives.

questions.2.opts: Lambrusco Mantovano is a dark Lambrusco whose grip the Codex never describes, so a guest could argue it as a second key. Salamino di Santa Croce, deep but round and soft in the Codex's reading, keeps the near miss with one key.
questions.2.exp: The explanation follows the new option and names both near misses.
open: The gumbo with andouille stays: the Codex's own pairing data makes a chilled dry Sorbara its model for a chilli dish, and the Creole dish is smoke, pork fat and gentle heat.
Rose petal beside violet rests on trade descriptions of Sorbara; left.
